prompt :
Use the uploaded image as the STRICT PRIMARY CHARACTER REFERENCE.

Create ONE ultra-detailed, professional UNIVERSAL CHARACTER SHEET in a wide 16:9 landscape format, following the exact structured production-reference layout described below.

The uploaded character may be MALE or FEMALE. Automatically analyze the reference image and preserve the person's exact visible identity, gender presentation, apparent age, facial structure, skin tone, hairstyle, hair color, body proportions, clothing, footwear and accessories.

CRITICAL IDENTITY LOCK:
Every single face and full-body view must depict THE EXACT SAME PERSON from the uploaded reference.

Do not redesign, beautify, age, de-age or replace the character.
No face drift.
No different person between angles.
No hairstyle drift.
No body-shape changes.
No outfit changes.

========================
TOP ROW — FACE TURNAROUND
========================

Create FIVE large, equally sized head-and-shoulder portrait panels:

1. FRONT FACE
Perfect straight-on facial view, looking toward camera.

2. LEFT 3/4 ANGLE
Natural approximately 45-degree left three-quarter view.

3. RIGHT 3/4 ANGLE
Natural approximately 45-degree right three-quarter view.

4. LEFT PROFILE
True 90-degree left-side facial profile.

5. RIGHT PROFILE
True 90-degree right-side facial profile.

All five portraits must maintain identical:
facial anatomy,
eye shape,
nose,
lips,
jaw,
ears,
skin tone,
hairline,
hairstyle,
apparent age and identity.

Use neutral expressions and clean studio lighting so the face can be used as an AI-film identity reference.

========================
TOP-RIGHT TITLE PANEL
========================

Create a clean premium typography panel:

UNIVERSAL
CHARACTER SHEET

Underneath:

SAME CHARACTER FOR ALL SCENES

Automatically generate a short visual description of the character's outfit/style based ONLY on the uploaded reference.

Do not invent story elements such as zombie, picnic, fantasy, occupation, etc. unless specifically supplied by the user.

========================
LEFT / LOWER SECTION — FULL BODY TURNAROUND
========================

Create FOUR large full-body studio views:

FULL BODY FRONT
FULL BODY LEFT SIDE
FULL BODY RIGHT SIDE
FULL BODY BACK

Show the complete character from top of head to bottom of shoes.

The front view must be genuinely straight-on.

Both side views must show accurate opposite sides of the SAME character.

The back view must be a true rear view.

Maintain EXACT SAME:
body proportions,
height impression,
hair,
clothing,
clothing fit,
fabric,
accessories,
shoes,
colors and physical identity.

Do not crop head or feet.

Natural relaxed standing posture.
Neutral production-reference poses.
No dramatic fashion posing.

========================
CENTER-RIGHT — OUTFIT DETAILS
========================

Create a section titled:

OUTFIT DETAILS

Generate SIX detailed macro/reference panels based on the ACTUAL outfit visible in the uploaded reference.

Examples depending on clothing:

TOP / SHIRT DETAIL
COLLAR DETAIL
POCKET DETAIL
SLEEVE DETAIL
LOWER GARMENT DETAIL
SHOE DETAIL

Automatically adapt labels to the actual wardrobe.

For example, if the character wears a dress, jacket, hoodie, suit, armor, traditional clothing, skirt, jeans, boots, etc., show details of those actual items.

Do NOT force the sample outfit.

Every detail must perfectly correspond to the clothing worn in the full-body images.

Show realistic:
stitching,
buttons,
zippers,
seams,
fabric folds,
wear,
material texture and construction.

========================
RIGHT COLUMN — PORTRAIT DETAILS
========================

Create a section titled:

PORTRAIT DETAILS

Generate SIX extreme close-up identity-reference panels:

LEFT EYE
RIGHT EYE
EYEBROW
NOSE
LIPS
SKIN DETAIL

These must come from the SAME character.

Eyes must preserve exact iris color and eye anatomy.

Nose and lips must preserve the character's unique shape.

Skin detail should show realistic pores, subtle texture and natural complexion.

No excessive beauty retouching.
No plastic skin.

These panels are intended to help preserve facial identity during future AI image/video generation.

========================
CHARACTER INFO
========================

Create a clean information box titled:

CHARACTER INFO

Automatically estimate ONLY visually reasonable information:

Gender Presentation:
Apparent Age Range:
Skin Tone:
Eye Color:
Hair Color:
Hair Style:
Body Type:
Outfit:
Style:
Makeup / Grooming:

Do NOT invent nationality, ethnicity, exact height, occupation or personal background when they cannot reliably be determined from appearance.

========================
COLOR PALETTE
========================

Create:

COLOR PALETTE

Display 5 clean rectangular swatches extracted directly from the character's actual outfit.

Use the dominant clothing/accessory colors.

Do not introduce unrelated colors.

========================
FABRIC TEXTURES
========================

Create:

FABRIC TEXTURES

Show FIVE realistic macro material samples derived from the actual outfit.

Examples:
cotton,
denim,
leather,
wool,
linen,
synthetic technical fabric,
knit,
shoe mesh,
metal accessory texture,
or other materials actually relevant to the reference.

These textures must visually match the clothing.

========================
LAYOUT LOCK
========================

The final image must look like ONE professionally designed Hollywood / Netflix production character-reference document.

Use a clean light-gray / off-white studio background.

Use thin elegant borders between panels.

Use refined black editorial typography.

Maintain strict grid alignment.

TOP:
5 facial-angle portraits + title/information panel.

BOTTOM-LEFT:
4 large full-body turnaround images.

CENTER-RIGHT:
6 outfit-detail panels.

FAR-RIGHT:
6 facial-detail macro panels + Character Info.

BOTTOM-CENTER:
Color Palette + Fabric Textures.

Do NOT replace this structure with a random collage.
Do NOT omit important sections.
Do NOT add environmental scenes.
Do NOT add unrelated props.
Do NOT add extra characters.

========================
PHOTOREALISM
========================

Pure photorealistic human appearance.
Professional studio photography.
Real human skin.
Natural pores and micro-texture.
Individual realistic hair strands.
Accurate anatomy.
Realistic hands and fingers.
Physically believable clothing.
High-end wardrobe photography.
Sharp facial details.
Soft controlled studio illumination.
Neutral color reproduction.
Premium editorial quality.

This is a CHARACTER CONTINUITY DOCUMENT, not fashion artwork.

The purpose is to allow the exact same digital actor to be recreated consistently in future AI films.

HIGHEST PRIORITY:
IDENTITY > FACIAL ACCURACY > BODY CONTINUITY > WARDROBE CONTINUITY > LAYOUT > BEAUTY.

ONE CHARACTER.
ONE FACE.
ONE BODY.
ONE OUTFIT.
ALL ANGLES.
ABSOLUTE CONTINUITY.

No text spelling errors where possible.
No distorted anatomy.
No duplicated limbs.
No extra fingers.
No mismatched eyes.
No asymmetrical accidental clothing changes.
No different shoes.
No outfit drift.
No identity drift.
No random accessories.
No watermark.

16:9 landscape.

8K: 7680 × 4320 ≈ 33.2 million pixels.

RL data 101: tasks

tasks have evolved over time. we started with preference pairs, where humans labeled right vs. wrong, A vs. B, and created simple demonstrations for SFT / pairs for DPO, these tasks aimed to engrave human taste into models. we then transitioned to more complex single-turn tasks. here, we turned to deterministic verifiers (RLVR) that are based on model rollouts. eventually, this evolved to multi-turn tasks with trajectories & deterministic + stochastic verifiers (LLMaaJ), which leads us to the current state of the data market. 

general make up of a task: input prompt, set of tools, environment + any custom seeding for that task, and verifiers. terminal bench is a relatively gold-standard for a normal coding task. 

ways i think about task creation (i'll do pitfalls later): 

> usefulness
>> to labs: 
>>> benchmark you're pegging the eval / data onto (Lab Y wants to hillclimb TBench, i make TBench-style data, that's immediately useful) 
>>> capability you're attaching the eval to (Lab Y wants to become better at legal, i make legal red-lining data, that's immediately useful) --> this is harder to prove but potentially more valuable 
>>> niche dataset that's impossible to get otherwise (real medical/company/session data), this is interesting especially pre-env creation, as raw data dumps 

>> the above are general principles in thinking about usefulness, but you should also be picking apart the traces / trajectories. the clear path to making a good task (post-env gen) is to: 
>>> you/LLM make the seed / think of the idea 
>>> you/LLM draft the task prompt, verifiers, constraints etc 
>>> run the task out, see score
>>> read the trajectory 
>>> if score hard enough + real + fair + accurate = good task 
>>> else: fix any issues in the task, regrade / re-rollout till you find it to be fair + accurate + a real task, difficulty comes last. a bad task that's hard is a bad task (net negative), a good task that's saturated is a good task (although worthless, net neutral). 

the specific things i'd look for in a rollout trace: 
> false positives 
> false negatives
> brittle / too strict of requirements (sub-string checks are an easy example for this, exact wording, function names, etc) 
>> a subset of this is naive verifiers. i.e. checking for very surface level reqs of a deep function, or not checking for large amounts of functionality or regressions (negative space criterion). this can lead to a model getting good at just the specific thing you want while regressing in surrounding functionality (i notice this a lot in early, less mature data recipes when im training my own models) 
> unfair verifiers and/or impossible requirements 
>> this can be an information issue, verifier issue, tool issue, or a prompt issue. 

one of the key reasons for the hugging face incident was impossible eval prompts led to the models breaking out while trying to find the answer because they couldn't solve it (i.e. bad task creation, catalyzed by bad tasks in training too). 

most of this is extremely hard for LLMs to do alone/autonomously, which is why really good engineers are still required for task creation.

The paper from ICLR26 targets a basic weakness of preference learning: a binary judgment such as “trajectory A is better than B” says nothing about why it is better, allowing a reward model to exploit incidental correlations—for example, learning that moving left is desirable when the actual preference is avoiding collisions. 

ReCouPLe uses the accompanying natural-language rationale as a geometric constraint: the rationale is embedded as a direction {\psi} and each trajectory representation {\phi(\tau)} is decomposed into a component parallel to that direction and an orthogonal residual, encouraging the preference to be explained by features aligned with the stated reason rather than unrelated context. 

The reported experiments show up to a 1.5× improvement in reward accuracy under distribution shift and roughly 2× downstream policy performance on novel tasks, while semantically shared reasons such as “avoids collisions” can be reused across tasks without additional language-model fine-tuning; the released implementation includes ManiSkill3, MetaWorld, and offline-RL components. 

The broader idea is more interesting than the specific algorithm: language may serve as structure in representation space, not merely as another supervision label. That creates a direct bridge to causal representation learning, concept bottlenecks, disentanglement and reward hacking, and suggests a possible extension to LLM alignment in which reward models learn separate, reusable directions for honesty, harmlessness, factuality or other stated reasons instead of compressing everything into one opaque scalar score. 

But the word “causal” needs care here: projecting onto a rationale embedding does not establish that the direction corresponds to a genuine causal variable in the interventionist sense, and incorrect or post-hoc human rationales could simply produce more robustly encoded mistakes. 

The most important next step is therefore an explicit intervention/counterfactual test—change only the factor named by a rationale while holding the rest of the trajectory fixed and test whether the associated reward direction changes as predicted. If that works, preference learning could move from fitting black-box scores toward learning interpretable, manipulable and compositional reward factors.
